_comment: Hand corrections to the OCR pass, folded in by tools/build_coords.py.
Positions are pixels of .build/a20/drawing_full.png (6120 x 2035) for the
board, and of .build/a20/schN_full.png for the sheets -- NOT of the
downscaled images the browser loads. The five sheets are all different
sizes, so sheetImageSize carries one entry per sheet.
_dropComment: Fifteen board markers the reader placed on another part's label. Every one
of the 126 markers it produced was rendered onto drawing_full.png and looked
at, tier by tier. The result:
agreed      85 of 85 correct
single       6 of 6  correct
ambiguous    6 of 9  correct
collision   13 of 26 correct
which is the pattern references/pitfalls.md predicts, with one pleasant
surprise: `agreed` was clean on this board, as it was on A12's, rather than
carrying the four bad markers A17's did. The collisions are all one shape --
two designators contesting a single silkscreen label, one of them right --
so they come in pairs: C1 landed on C126, C104 on C109, C124 on C129, C14
and C16 on C10 and C11, C15 on C152, C9 and C4 on C2 and C9, R7 on C131,
U1 on TP5, U2 on U20, U5 on U8, U4 on U41.
These are dropped rather than nudged, because a marker on a neighbour's
label is worse than no marker: it sends a probe to the wrong part and it
makes the coverage badge lie in the comfortable direction. Dropped, they
count as unplaced, which is the truth. Placing them by hand is outstanding
work and is listed as such in the report.
T1 and DS1 are a different case and are also in notOnDrawing below: they are
Series II designators for parts this build calls T51 and CR1, so there is no
silkscreen anywhere on this drawing for them to sit on. The reader's DS1
marker had merged several unrelated reads and spanned a third of the board,
which is the A18 MP2 and A19 H7 failure again -- a truncation or a merge
quietly promoting a part with no designator into one that looks placed.
That outstanding work is now done: C1, C4, C9, C104, C124, U1, U2, U4 and U5
are hand-placed in the board block below, on the labels and outlines that are
actually theirs. They stay listed here because the entry records what the
reader got wrong, and build_coords.py prefers a hand placement over a read in
any case. C14, C15, C16 and R7 stay dropped and are now in notOnDrawing as
well: the reader's reads for them were on C10, C11, C152 and C131, and the
parts themselves are Series II surface-mount and not on this build.
_notOnDrawingComment: Parts with no silkscreen designator on the locator drawing. Counting them
as unplaced would make the coverage badge lie and send someone hunting for
a rivet that was never drawn. Three groups:
The IC sockets X5, X6, X8, X10, X13 and X15-X24. A socket has no
designator of its own -- it sits under the IC it holds and is named after
it. Fourteen of them, and they are the reason this board can be repaired
at all: every EPROM, the RAM, the EEPROM and the processor are socketed.
The hardware: H3-H6 (rivets), M3/M4 (adhesive rubber feet), MP1/MP2 (the
nylon ejector ears) and MP7/MP8 (adhesive pads). None is drawn with a
designator. Note MP1 means two different things in the two parts lists --
the bare printed circuit board in the Series II list, an ejector in Rev
9's -- and neither has a silkscreen label either way.
DS1 and XBT1, which are Series II surface-mount parts that do not exist
on this build at all. The reset lamp here is CR1 and the cell is soldered
in at BT1, so there is no DS1 or XBT1 footprint on the drawing to place
them on. They stay in the parts list because a Series II board would need
them.
The Series II surface-mount parts that this build simply does not have:
C7, C14, C15, C16, C18, C107, C142 (0.1uF 0805 bypass), R2 and R7 (zero
ohm 1206), R8 and R9 (75R) and R10-R17 (10K and 1K 1206). Every one is in
the 1996 Series II list with no as-built counterpart in Rev 9, and that
turns out to be the whole rule on this board: of the 28 parts listed only
as Series II, the 26 that are not test points appear on neither the
drawing nor any of the five sheets, while every Series II part that does
carry an as-built row is placed. The through-hole build does the same job
with the resistor networks Z1-Z5, which is visible on sheet 1 as 4.7K
network sections where the SMD board had discretes. Each was searched for
with find_in_image over the whole drawing and looked at in full-resolution
crops; the reader's own hits for them on sheets 1-5 were rendered and are
every one a pin or port label -- R16 on A16, R17 on A17, R2 on A21, C14 on
D14, C15 on D15, C16 on CLK, C18 on D10, C7 on the O7 pin of U15.
R81, which is the odd one out: it is in the Rev 9 list, not the Series II
one, sharing stock number 573030 and a quantity of two with R82. Only one
150R footprint is drawn, and it is labelled R82; sheet 4 likewise shows a
single R82 150 across the 3.6864MHZCLK output. find_in_image found no R81
on the drawing or on sheet 4 and no reader pass on any of the six images
produced one. Recorded here as a parts-list-to-artwork discrepancy rather
than hunted for further.
_boardComment: Every test point placed by hand, which is the rule rather than a reaction to
a bad read: on this drawing the pad is a short dash 40-75 px from its
silkscreen number, and a marker centred on the number sends a probe to the
wrong place. Each box below spans the number and the pad together, measured
off a 50 px grid over drawing_full.png.
Nine were measured pad and label: TP1, TP3, TP4, TP5, TP7, TP8, TP9, TP10
and TP11. Four -- TP6, TP12, TP13 and TP14 -- are the reader's verified
label box widened by a margin, because their pads could not be told apart
from neighbouring artwork at the grid resolution used: TP6's from SW1's
switch outline, and TP13/TP14's from the polarity marking under BT1. Those
four are honest to within about 60 px and are flagged here rather than
presented as measurements.
TP4 and TP9 needed placing outright as well as widening. TP4's only read was
on TP1's label at the far left of the board, 5 000 px from where it belongs,
and TP9 was never found at all -- the same TP9 blind spot A18 hit, where the
reader takes the 9 for an S.
The thirteen sit in four groups: TP1 alone at the top left corner, TP3 and
TP8 together left of centre, TP12 alone above U23, TP4-TP7 and TP9-TP11 in
the row across the top right beside SW1 and U1, and TP13/TP14 across the
battery BT1. That matches the sheet 1 legend's own page references, which
put TP1 and TP3 on sheet 1, TP4-TP8 on sheet 4 and TP9-TP14 on sheet 5.
Below the test points, nineteen parts the reader either misplaced or never
found at all. Two shapes, following the drawing: where the designator is
printed inside a component outline the marker is that outline -- the DIPs U1,
U2, U4, U5, U9, U27, U32 and the resistor network Z2, the transformer can
T51, and the two electrolytics C1 and C17 as circles -- and where it is
printed beside its part the marker is a tight box on the text, sized like the
board's other label markers: C4, C9, C104, C122, C124, C133, CR4 and CR7.
The outlines were flood-filled from the designator and the circles measured
from the ink extent; every one was rendered onto drawing_full.png and looked
at before it was written here.

_dropSchematicComment: Sheet 1 was reviewed marker by marker; sheets 2 to 5 were not, and everything
on them is dropped rather than shipped unchecked. That is a deliberate
decision and the reason is measured, not assumed.
On sheet 1 the reader placed 79 markers. Reviewing them gave:
agreed tier   14 of 31 correct
test points    1 of 11 correct
-- about 60% wrong in the *best* tier, which is worse than the third-to-half
references/pitfalls.md leads you to expect and squarely in A14's territory.
Every failure mode the pitfalls file names is here in one sheet:
Pin and port labels read as designators. This is the dominant one on a
processor board, because the sheets are wall-to-wall pin numbers: TP4 landed
on U5's IO4 pin, TP6 on IO6, TP8 on IO8, TP9 on IO2, M4 on I12, R16 on A16,
R17 on A17, R2 on A21, C13 on D13, C15 on D15, P61 on D11, U25 on D05,
U27 on D07, U10 on IPL1*/IPL2*, TP7 on D12. Every one of those is a real
designator on this board sitting on a pin label that merely looks like it.
The test point legend block, which is the offender the pitfalls file warns
arrives looking trustworthy. The thirteen-line 'TP1 = CLK (PG1D5)' table in
the top right corner produced markers for TP10, TP12, TP13 and TP14 that
point at the table rather than at a net. build_coords.py's own legend
detector caught exactly these four and said so; the rest of the table's
damage it could not see.
A second legend block the detector knows nothing about: the SPARES box,
where the unused sections of the resistor networks are drawn. Z3 and Z5
both landed there. The designator is right and the position answers a
question nobody asked -- Z3's working sections are all over the sheet.
A caption read as a designator: C2 landed on the 'ON' of 'EXCEPTION VECTOR
PULLUPS'.
Fourteen sheet 1 markers survived review and are kept: C104, C106, C109 and
C111 in the bypass row, C8 and C9 at the crystal, CR1 at the not-reset
indicator, R3 and R4, TP3 on the ECLK flag (the only test point the reader
got right anywhere), U6, U8, U11 and Y1. Those are the parts §2-31 and §2-32
name for the reset and clock circuits, which is the half of this sheet a
technician actually opens.
Sheets 2 to 5 are dropped wholesale. Their reader output is versioned so the
review can be done from exactly these reads without re-running tesseract --
that is what the .build/a20 stanza in .gitignore is for -- but shipping ~200
unreviewed markers of which, on this evidence, more than half would be wrong
is worse than shipping none: a wrong marker on a sheet sends a probe to the
wrong net while the badge calls it 'agreed'.
_sheetsComment: The zone grid of each sheet, measured off the printed frame: columns 8 to 1
left to right and rows D to A top to bottom, with 'frame' the inner border
in normalised sheet coordinates. Zone labels for every placement are derived
from these rather than typed, which also makes them checkable against the
page/zone references the sheet 1 test point legend prints for all thirteen
_layersComment: Registration of the photograph against the locator drawing, from which
build_coords.py solves the board -> photo homography. 'src' is board space
(the drawing), 'dst' is photo space; both are normalised, not pixels.
Every 'src' below is a board position already reviewed marker by marker and
sitting in the 'board' block above, so each pair is a correspondence someone
can check -- open the drawing at C123 and the photograph at C123 and see the
same spot -- rather than a sample of a matrix. The matching 'dst' was found
by cross-correlation: the locator drawing *is* the silkscreen artwork and the
photograph shows the same artwork in yellow ink, so a yellow-ink mask of the
photo (R-B, which keeps the silkscreen and drops the blue board, the black
packages and the white EPROM labels) was matched patch by patch against the
drawing's own ink, and the fit re-solved and re-matched until it stopped
moving. None of the landmarks is on a designator's *text*: the drawing prints
much of that inside the part outline where the board prints it outside, so a
300 px patch is matched on the outlines around the point and the offset that
wins is applied to the reviewed coordinate.
Nothing here is on an ejector lever, a mounting hole or a standoff. Both of
this board's levers are photographed swung out of their stowed position, so
besides standing proud of the PCB the way references/pitfalls.md warns about,
they are not even where the drawing draws them.
How good it is, measured rather than asserted. The same cross-correlation was
run at all 112 reviewed board positions; 79 of them peaked unambiguously and
are the population the fit was judged against. Against those 79 the shipped
homography lands a median 4.8 px, p90 8.6 px and worst 13.4 px out, in pixels
of the 3400 px photo the browser loads -- comparable with A19's 3.7/11.2/15.0
and better than A9's 9.2/23.9/24.1. The 26 landmarks kept below are one per
cell of a 10x3 grid over the board, chosen by peak sharpness, and the
homography they give agrees with the one fitted to all 79 to within 3.5 px
everywhere on the board -- i.e. the fit is anchored across the whole board
rather than in one region and extrapolated.
The residual that is left is not noise and does not come out with more
landmarks: it is a smooth field that changes sign along the board, which is
the signature of the scan of a D-size drawing rather than of the camera. No
single projective transform removes it. It is worst at the right-hand end,
where fitting the middle alone would have put the R52-R61/CR1-CR8 column 20
px out; the fit below spreads that error instead of concentrating it.
Checked the way that actually catches a bad fit: all 112 reviewed markers
were drawn onto the photograph through this homography and looked at, from
C108/TP1/R5 at the left edge through U15-U22 and P61/P62 in the middle to
TP9/CR1-CR8/R52-R61/U52/Z4/C145 at the right. Every one lands on its own
part.
